claims.text: Pre-coating tungsten particles with a nanoscale WC layer before copper infiltration will increase the thermal conductivity of a W–Cu composite relative to an otherwise comparable composite with uncoated tungsten particles.
The WC-coated W–Cu composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to that of the uncoated control.
The WC-coated W–Cu composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to that of the uncoated control.
Applying a controlled nanoscale WC coating to tungsten particles before composite processing will create a thin, continuous WC interphase at the W–Cu boundary.
The WC interphase will act as a graded interface between tungsten and copper.
The WC interphase will reduce vibrational or phonon mismatch between tungsten and copper.
The WC interphase will reduce interfacial scattering at the W–Cu boundary.
Reduced vibrational mismatch and interfacial scattering will lower thermal boundary resistance.
Lower thermal boundary resistance will increase the overall thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
WC has inherent hardness that can help preserve the mechanical durability of the composite.
WC has inherent irradiation stability that can help preserve the irradiation resistance of the composite.
The predicted benefit should hold under high thermal flux, mechanical loading, and irradiation conditions representative of heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
The beneficial effect depends on the WC coating having an optimized nanoscale thickness, being continuous, and remaining intact during operation.
An excessively thick WC coating may act as a thermal barrier and negate the conductivity benefit.
A discontinuous or mechanically unstable WC coating may crack under stress and negate the proposed benefits.
